items.title: Combining transcriptomics, single-cell data, and a combination of 113-combination machine learning framework, as well as experimental verification, identified the key genes related to lactylation modifications in ulcerative colitis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by immune dysregulation and mucosal inflammation. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying UC by identifying key genetic markers and potential therapeutic targets.The GSE75214 dataset was used for differential expression analysis, and candidate genes were identified through cross-validation with known lactylation-related genes (LRGs). Enrichment analysis combined with protein-protein interaction (PPI) network assessment revealed that these genes are likely involved in the pathogenic mechanisms of UC. Machine learning techniques, particularly glmBoost combined with linear discriminant analysis (LDA), identified four key candidate genes: CNN2, HSDL2, LDHB, and S100A6. These findings were validated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, which yielded area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.7 in both the training and validation datasets, underscoring their potential as biomarkers for UC. Immune infiltration analysis demonstrated significant disparities in the abundance of 26 distinct immune cell types between normal and disease cohorts, underscoring the intricate relationship between immune response and disease progression. Regulatory networks involving transcription factors and microRNAs were explored to understand the molecular mechanisms of these interactions. Drug prediction analysis identified specific drugs, particularly valproic acid, isoproterenol, and acetaminophen, underscoring the translational potential of this study in targeted therapeutic strategies. Molecular docking studies further confirmed the efficacy of these interactions. Data analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) revealed that undifferentiated cells were the key cell type, and there were significant differences in the expression of four key genes.This analysis has enhanced our understanding of the molecular basis of UC and also provided guidance for subsequent research and clinical applications. Clinical trial number: not applicable

items.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
items.abstract_or_text: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.

items.title: MedMCP: An Open Agentic Ecosystem for Medical Imaging Workflows
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning has driven rapid progress in medical image analysis, with methods for tasks such as organ segmentation, anomaly detection, and radiology report generation now matching or surpassing expert performance on several benchmarks. While many methods are released as open source, their routine adoption by clinicians and medical researchers remains limited. The bottleneck is not a lack of capable tools, but the absence of infrastructure to make them accessible to non-technical users. To break this barrier, we present MedMCP, an agentic framework that solves this last-mile problem along two axes: (1) a local agentic workspace that lets users apply state-of-the-art image analysis methods through natural language, and (2) a community-driven tool ecosystem that lets developers deploy and distribute capabilities as validated, independently testable servers. MedMCP enforces a strict orchestration-execution boundary in which a local language model translates user intent into workflow plans, while all image analysis is delegated to domain-specific tools. The framework runs entirely on-premise, every side-effecting operation passes through a human-in-the-loop permission gate, and a full provenance trail links each output to the tools, parameters, and inputs that produced it. An inspectable workspace lets users verify intermediate results rather than blindly trusting the agent, and completed sessions distill into deterministic, shareable workflows that re-execute without the agent, turning one-off interactions into reproducible analyses. This paper introduces the project's general idea and describes the design principles that guide its development. Beyond a single toolkit, we envision MedMCP as a community-driven platform where each contributed tool becomes easily accessible, compounding individual efforts into shared capability.

items.title: A synthetic MALDI-TOF MS atlas for microbial classification across hospitals
items.abstract_or_text: Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry (MS) is central to routine clinical microbiology for species identification. Its combination with machine learning is constrained by fragmented public datasets, species imbalance and acquisition-related variability. Synthetic datasets could provide more training data, but they must preserve the spectral information needed to make predictions on real samples. Here, we present an open, synthetic MALDI-TOF MS atlas comprising 4.3 million spectra across 43 clinically relevant bacterial species. To construct the atlas, we harmonised public repositories from three countries and trained a species- and institution-conditioned concept-bottleneck generative variational autoencoder (CBGM-VAE) on 179,086 measured spectra. We assessed the atlas as both a stand-alone training resource and a complement to real data, using bacterial species classification as a functional benchmark. Evaluation comprised 7,269 real spectra from more than 7 countries, 24 institutions and multiple acquisition platforms, covering: temporal, technical, biological and combined shifts. A neural network trained only on synthetic spectra achieved F1 scores ranging from 0.788 to 1.000 across external cohorts. When synthetic spectra were combined with real training data, classification performance improved or matched using real data only. These findings demonstrate that the atlas retains transferable information and can complement measured data. The openly released atlas provides a reusable resource for supervised learning and benchmarking. It can also be explored for pretraining representation-learning and foundation models in MALDI-TOF MS research.

items.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Surgical Education: Comparing AI- and Surgeon-Generated Feedback in Informed Consent Training
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Purpose: Informed consent (IC) is a complex communication competency requiring procedural knowledge, patient-centered decision-making, and nuanced risk-benefit communication. Large language models (LLMs) offer scalable opportunities for simulated IC training and individualized feedback; however, their ability to accurately evaluate learner performance remains insufficiently validated. We compared AI- and surgeon-generated evaluations of simulated IC encounters to assess performance score alignment and narrative feedback quality. Methods: Six medical students completed an LLM-based simulated appendectomy consent incorporating a culturally sensitive scenario. Each transcript received one AI- and four surgeon-generated evaluations using a 17-item IC rubric. Scoring alignment was defined as the difference between AI-assigned and surgeon-assigned scores. Feedback quality was evaluated using an 8-item modified Completed Clinical Evaluation Report Rating (mCCERR) framework assessing comprehensiveness and balance, specificity and justification, and educational utility and constructiveness. Results AI assigned higher performance scores than surgeons, with significant differences in addressing patient emotions, explaining the procedure, risks, and alternatives, and avoiding coercion (all P = 0.03). The largest absolute differences included explaining contraindications, assessing capacity, and integrating patient preferences. AI-generated feedback received significantly higher quality ratings, with a higher median overall mCCERR score than surgeon-generated feedback (38.5 vs 24.75, P = 0.04). Conclusions LLMs generated high-quality, comprehensive feedback but demonstrated systematic discordance with surgeon assessment, consistently assigning more favorable performance scores. These findings demonstrate that high feedback quality should not be viewed as a proxy for greater evaluative validity. LLMs may be well-suited for repeated simulated practice and individualized formative feedback but should be paired with human oversight for nuanced assessment of IC proficiency.

items.title: Machine learning and single-cell transcriptomics identify key lncRNAs associated with malignant transformation and immune infiltration in colorectal cancer
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background : Colorectal cancer (CRC) is generally thought to arise through the normal–adenoma–tumor sequence. Which long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) change at each step, and whether these coincide with immune-cell infiltration, remain incompletely characterized. Methods: Three microarray datasets with normal, adenoma and tumor samples (GSE37364, GSE100179, GSE117606) were analyzed. Seven algorithms were combined into 120 models to form a two-layer classifier separating normal from diseased tissue and adenoma from tumor. Immune-cell fractions were estimated with CIBERSORT; candidates were examined in single-cell data (GSE201349; 46,562 cells) and for progression-free survival (PFS) in 357 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Results : Seven lncRNAs were identified: UCA1, RTEL1-TNFRSF6B, LOC102724156, GATA2-AS1, SATB2-AS1, H19 and BLOC1S1-RDH5. First-layer accuracy, area under the curve (AUC) and F-score were 0.972, 0.979 and 0.978; second-layer values were 0.958, 0.958 and 0.955. M0 macrophages and activated dendritic cells were enriched in diseased tissue and correlated with five lncRNAs (all P Conclusions : These seven lncRNAs form a two-layer classifier separating normal, adenoma and tumor tissue, but none of the six measurable there was associated with PFS after correction. They are candidate tissue biomarkers for staging along the normal–adenoma–tumor sequence rather than markers of prognosis.

items.title: Integrative transcriptomic and machine learning analyses identify ABCD1 as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in cutaneous melanoma
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM) is highly aggressive and heterogeneous, and robust biomarkers remain limited. We integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data with machine learning to identify key driver genes and prognostic markers in SKCM. Methods This study integrated transcriptomic data from two GEO cohorts, GSE15605 and GSE46517, together with the TCGA-SKCM cohort to identify consistently differentially expressed genes. Four machine learning algorithms, including LASSO, SVM-RFE, XGBoost, and Boruta, were then applied to systematically screen core candidate genes. Publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data from GSE125121 were further analyzed to determine the cellular origin of these core genes. Survival analysis and clinicopathological correlation analysis were performed to evaluate the clinical relevance and potential therapeutic value of ABCD1. Finally, the protein expression of ATP-binding cassette subfamily D member 1 (ABCD1) was validated by Western blot. Results We identified 866 consistently differentially expressed genes and five robust candidates: ABCD1, KIF3C, CNNM1, TRIB1, and NT5DC3. Single-cell analysis showed that these genes were mainly enriched in malignant melanoma cells and displayed marked intratumoral heterogeneity. Among them, ABCD1 exhibited the broadest and highest expression across malignant subpopulations. Pseudotime analysis indicated that ABCD1 and NT5DC3 were predominantly associated with terminal malignant states, whereas TRIB1 spanned transitional and terminal states. In TCGA-SKCM, high ABCD1 expression was significantly associated with worse overall survival, while the other genes showed limited prognostic value. Western blot further showed that ABCD1 protein expression was low in normal skin, nevus, and stage I SKCM tissues, but markedly increased in stage II–III SKCM tissues Conclusions ABCD1 is a promising prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target in SKCM. This multi-omics framework provides a robust strategy for biomarker discovery in melanoma.

items.title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
items.abstract_or_text: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman ρ= -0.065, n = 300, 95% CI [-0.18, +0.05]; distance correlation = 0.10, independence test p = 0.24). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff α is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.

items.title: Prioritization of Androgenetic Alopecia-Associated Lactylation Sites through Multi-Omics Integration and the HybridKla Deep Learning Framework
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract The contribution of lysine lactylation to androgenetic alopecia (AGA) remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated scalp single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, lactylomics, and HybridKla-based deep learning to prioritize AGA-associated lactylation candidates. Single-cell data from three frontal–occipital donor pairs provided a T-cell-related transcriptional context, while proteomic and lactylomic profiling of two donor pairs identified 1,804 lactylation sites on 551 proteins. ZBTB7B, a transcription factor involved in T-cell lineage regulation, showed opposing regional trends in total-protein and modified-peptide abundance: frontal-to-occipital ratios were 1.806 for total ZBTB7B, 0.523 for K206-associated lactylated peptides, and 0.587 for K212-associated lactylated peptides. These directions were consistent across both donors, although neither site passed multiple-testing correction. To support candidate prioritization, we adapted HybridKla using 46,403 reference site records with protein-grouped five-fold partitioning for base-model evaluation. Five-score fusion yielded reported receiver operating characteristic and precision–recall areas under the curve of 0.8281 and 0.7984, respectively. Classification-head adaptation increased mean recall from 78.09% to 90.75% on 346 confirmed positive sites from 176 held-out proteins; this positive-only evaluation assessed detection sensitivity rather than overall classification performance. Both K206 and K212 were included among predicted-positive ZBTB7B sites and supported by mass-spectrometric localization records. Together, these findings prioritize ZBTB7B K206 and K212 as candidate sites for investigating lactylation-associated regulation in AGA. The integrated workflow connects tissue-level observations with residue-specific evidence, providing a focused basis for examining post-translational regulation within the follicular immune microenvironment.

items.title: Metric-dependent evaluation of a retrieval-augmented large language model workflow for oral squamous cell carcinoma treatment planning: a retrospective study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but open-ended treatment planning poses a measurement problem: a clinically defensible recommendation may differ from a historical plan, and different automated metrics may reward different properties of the same output. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) may improve evidence grounding, but its contribution cannot be inferred without controlled ablation. We evaluated how four archived RAG-enabled LLM configurations agreed with clinician treatment plans for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and whether apparent model ranking depended on the evaluation method. Methods This single-center retrospective evaluation used the same 100-case OSCC study set for four archived configurations (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Doubao, and Qwen). Generated treatment plans were compared with archived clinician plans using a DeepSeek-based LLM-judge score, m3e-base embedding cosine similarity, ROUGE-1 recall, and an archived blinded five-physician rating protocol. Cohort descriptors were audited from the de-identified case register. Because complete case-level metric arrays and the case-by-rater matrix were not retained, model comparisons were summarized descriptively and no unsupported paired inference was reconstructed. Results The cohort had a mean age of 59.5 years (SD 13.6); 65% of cases were male and 69% were source-coded N0. Model ordering differed by automated metric: Qwen had the highest mean LLM-judge score (0.809; DeepSeek-R1, 0.807), Doubao had the highest mean embedding similarity (0.8489), and Claude had the highest mean ROUGE-1 recall (0.2729). No configuration was uniformly best. The archived clinician-rating summary showed a different descriptive pattern, but formal inter-rater reliability and paired model comparisons could not be recomputed from the available archive. Conclusions In this retrospective OSCC treatment-planning evaluation, apparent model performance was inseparable from the reference standard and evaluation method. The findings support feasibility of the combined RAG-enabled workflow and demonstrate the limitations of selecting a clinical LLM from a single aggregate metric; they do not establish clinical equivalence, autonomous safety, patient benefit, or a causal advantage of RAG. Future validation should use time-aligned evidence, locked system configurations, independent clinical adjudication, paired case-level analyses, severity-weighted safety assessment, controlled RAG ablation, and clinician-in-the-loop prospective evaluation.

items.title: Variable sparsity non-negative matrix and tensor factorization algorithms and their applications in cancer genomics
items.abstract_or_text: The field of oncology has experienced significant advancements in novel therapies and molecular diagnostics to personalize initial cancer treatments. However, cancer's propensity for evolution and resistance to therapies remains a formidable challenge due to its dynamic nature. Cancer's complex and adaptive behavior surpasses the capabilities of simple models, complicating our comprehension at every level, from basic sciences to clinical practices, highlighting the urgent need for innovative approaches to improve the modeling and classification of cancer. In this context, matrix factorization algorithms have been used to generate transcriptional signatures that summarize the most salient patterns of behaviors in cancer datasets. For example, the standard non-negative matrix factorization algorithm (NMF) generates a dimensionality-reduced representation that encodes a significant amount of data relationships as a mixture of positive components and provides a working summary of the input data. The resulting NMF factor matrices, W and H, display some degree of sparseness; however, this sparseness is often a byproduct rather than an explicit objective of the NMF algorithm, and the user has limited control over the degree of sparseness of the representation and the corresponding balance between local versus global structures in the NMF results. Some sparse versions of NMF have been introduced but still do not allow a fine-grained control on the sparsity constraints. We present here a novel variable-sparsity Non-negative Matrix Factorization algorithm (vsNMF), where instead of imposing sparsity as a regularization constraint on the NMF objective function, sparsity is explicitly enforced by a projective step performed for each column of W and row of H after a standard NMF update. In this way, the algorithm takes as input the input matrix, plus two one-dimensional vectors, that specify the sparsity functions that will be imposed on the NMF solution. The more explicit control of sparsity, and the corresponding balance between local vs. global structure, at the level of individual components, allows the generation of NMF solutions that can be tuned to operate anywhere between a generative, parts-based encoding of overlapping features, and a partitional, soft-clustering model. This allows greater flexibility to represent biological subtypes, patterns of pathway activation or deregulation, and higher biological interpretability. These learned low-dimensionality representations can also be used to integrate and merge datasets, or to define groups of similar cancer samples representing putative cellular or tumor states. Adjustable/tunable NMF representations of biological data can greatly help advance our fundamental understanding of cancer biology, provide more interpretable computational models of cancer, and better functional cancer taxonomies and precision oncology paradigms. We apply the same approach to tensors and introduce a variable-sparsity Non-Negative Tensor Factorization algorithm (vsNTF) that can take an input tensor and sparsity functions for each of the tensor dimensions.

items.title: Optimization-Based Adaptive Hybrid Biomarker Selection with Explainable Attention 1D-CNN for Early Ovarian Cancer Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Precise and interpretable biomarker selection is crucial for early diagnosis of diseases and precision medicine. Nonetheless, high-dimensional biomedical datasets are characteristically having redundant, noisy, and correlated features, thereby deteriorating classification performance and interpretability. A NEW Effective Optimization-Based Adaptive Hybrid Biomarker Selection Framework (O-AHBS) Integrated with an Attention-Enhanced Multi-Scale 1D Convolutional Neural Network for Diagnosing Biological Classification in Biomedical Applications is Proposed; the method gives input to AMS-1D-CNN robustly. We propose an open-source hybrid scoring approach called O-AHBS that uniquely combines statistical feature ranking, ensemble-based feature importance, and explainability-driven inference into a comprehensive scoring system. PSO learns the weights for scoring from data itself, which allows us to choose discriminative biomarkers. An attention-boosted multi-scale 1D-CNN that emphasises clinically relevant biomarker interactions is then used to classify the chosen biomarkers. We performed stratified 10-fold cross-validation and compared the framework with XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Evaluation was done using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, balanced accuracy, and ROC-AUC. Statistical significance was ensured using the Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests, while global and local interpretability were facilitated by SHAP and LIME. Comparative experimental results validate the proposed framework to deliver higher predictive accuracy, robustness, and interpretability than state-of-the-art methods, thus ensuring its potential role as an effective decision-support tool for biomarker-driven disease diagnosis.

items.title: Cross-Dimension and Cross-Modality Relational Tensor Representation Learning for Multimodal Health Data Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Multimodal health data integrate information from heterogeneous clinical sources, creating substantial opportunities for data-driven decision support. Realizing these opportunities, however, requires effectively modeling complex dependencies that arise both within individual modalities and across modalities. This paper proposes Relational Tensor Representation (RTR), a unified framework that jointly learns dimension-specific tensor representations and cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships. RTR introduces learnable relational bridge matrices that maintain relational information while preserving the structural identities of tensor dimensions and modalities. A structured fusion mechanism further integrates factor-level and relationship-level information into compact representations for downstream prediction. Experiments on simulated data and two multimodal neurophysiological datasets, covering emotion recognition and brain activity classification, demonstrate that RTR consistently outperforms representative tensor learning, multimodal fusion, and Transformer-based baselines. These results highlight the value of explicitly modeling cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships for learning informative representations from heterogeneous multimodal tensor data. The source code is planned for public release to support reproducibility and future research.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT) on Medical Decision-Making in the Healthcare System of Afghanistan
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into clinical practice is altering medical decision-making. While many studies evaluate the theoretical accuracy of models like ChatGPT in high-resource settings, data on their real-world deployment in developing nations remains scarce. This research investigates the practical use, perceived accuracy, and safety of ChatGPT in Afghanistan's healthcare system, a sector facing severe resource limits and a shortage of specialists. We conducted a cross-sectional quantitative survey of 42 medical professionals in Kabul's public and private clinics. We evaluated four main clinical metrics: Appropriateness, Patient Usefulness, Safety, and Alignment with Guidelines. Survey results show a high adoption rate among early-career physicians (66.7% having under six years of experience), who mainly use the tool for general medical information and interpreting lab tests. While ChatGPT scored highly for patient education, practitioners reported significant reservations about clinical safety. Specialists, especially surgeons and internists, raised concerns about AI hallucinations during complex diagnoses and treatments. Despite these risks, 59.5% of the surveyed doctors believe AI will improve the Afghan healthcare system by filling information gaps. We conclude that while ChatGPT is a helpful information tool, its safe use requires strict human oversight and the development of clear clinical guidelines.

items.title: Generative Retrieval for Reverse Target Fishing with a Proteome-Scale Benchmark
items.abstract_or_text: Reverse target fishing identifies protein targets for a query molecule and is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Discriminative approaches adapted from virtual screening face sparse, long-tailed associations and missing-not-at-random measurements: treating unrecorded pairs as negatives can suppress genuine targets. We reformulate the task as generative retrieval and introduce GenFish. Residual vector quantization converts frozen protein language model features into shared semantic identifiers. Given a molecular fingerprint, GenFish autoregressively models codes conditioned on the query and preceding code, ranking proteins by identifier likelihood without explicitly labeling unrecorded pairs as negatives. We introduce ProTargetBench, the first proteome-scale benchmark for reverse target fishing to jointly support measured-panel discrimination and full-catalogue recovery of experimentally recorded positives. Covering 20,431 UniProt-reviewed human proteins, it integrates curated bioactivity evidence and distinguishes experimental inactivity from unmeasured associations. On 198 held-out molecules, GenFish achieves higher mean performance across all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics than four discriminative neural baselines and three non-neural baselines, including ligand-based methods. A controlled positive-hiding experiment shows that targeted removal of false-negative competition improves contrastive retrieval beyond matched random masking; GenFish remains stronger under the same incomplete supervision. Pfam alignment indicates that the semantic identifiers capture biologically meaningful relationships among proteins. These results establish generative retrieval as a principled paradigm for reverse target fishing under incomplete bioactivity records.

items.title: Predicting cell-state-specific gene regulation from DNA across species
items.abstract_or_text: DNA encodes the cell's phenotype, but the same DNA sequence is interpreted differently in every cell type, developmental stage, and activity state. Existing deep-learning models solve only half of this puzzle: sequence-to-function models read DNA but treat cell state as a fixed label, while single-cell foundation models represent cell state but not sequence. We developed Bolero, a sequence-to-function model whose parameters condition on atlas-scale cell-state embeddings and additional biological variables to predict cell-state-specific chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance from DNA. Trained on 10.7 million cells from 33 datasets across six mammals, Bolero matched or exceeded specialised models and resolved regulatory differences between closely related cell states, including cortical regional and developmental gradients. Extrapolating cell-state embeddings extended Bolero's predictions to cell states that are absent from training. Cell-state conditioning facilitated tracing of the effects of non-coding variants to the cell types in which they act. Using an AP-1 activity score as a further continuous conditioning axis, Bolero predicted activity-regulated chromatin changes without requiring actual stimulation data. Across human cell types, we reconstructed the cooperative grammar of motif identity and spacing underlying predicted AP-1 responses. Bolero further predicted cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and AP-1 responses in species excluded from training, extending comparative genomics from sequence conservation to predicted functional conservation. Across 84 mammals, we found that predicted AP-1 responses were less conserved than chromatin accessibility at cis-regulatory elements, driven by the human-specific sequence variants on AP-1 and cooperating motifs. By combining reference genomes with reference cell atlases, Bolero allowed genome sequences, either native or mutated, to be queried across cell states, perturbations, and different species for their chromatin and expression signatures.

items.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

items.title: Machine Learning for Predicting Somatic Cell Count in Holstein Cattle
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Somatic cell count (SCC) is a key indicator of udder health and milk quality in dairy cattle, but predicting it from routinely recorded data is difficult because SCC is highly skewed and depends on production, reproductive, and management factors that interact with one another. Seven modeling approaches were evaluated for predicting natural log-transformed SCC (LSCC) in Holstein cows using data from a commercial dairy herd. The approaches included Multiple Regression (MR) and Generalized Linear Model (GLM) as linear benchmark methods, a Support Vector Machine (SVM) using a Radial Basis Function kernel, and four nonlinear methods, including Bayesian Neural Network (BNN), Random Forest (RF), Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID), and Classification and Regression Tree (C&R Tree). After multivariate outlier removal, 9,915 records were retained and stratified into five lactation groups, and models were developed using on-farm data. Nonlinear models generally showed higher testing correlations and lower relative errors than MR, GLM, and SVM. The best-performing models achieved testing correlations of approximately 0.62 to 0.70 across the first four lactation groups, whereas predictive performance declined in cows with more than four lactations. BNN and RF showed broadly comparable predictive performance across lactation groups. Average protein, milk, and fat yields were among the most influential predictors of LSCC in both models, with average milk yield becoming the most important predictor in cows with more than four lactations. Overall, nonlinear models, particularly BNN and RF, provided better prediction of LSCC from routinely recorded data than the conventional approaches, although prediction accuracy decreased in later lactations.

items.title: Structured Metabolic Genetic Axes Reveal Distinct Lipid and Ketone-Body Programs in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Metabolic dysregulation has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD), yet circulating metabolites are embedded within highly correlated metabolic networks. This structure complicates single-metabolite analyses and motivates genetic approaches that model shared metabolic architecture directly. Methods We applied Genomic SEM to NMR metabolite GWAS summary statistics to construct lipid and non-lipid latent metabolic factor GWAS. Six factors were screened against AD, PD, and Lewy body dementia using cross-trait LDSC, followed by MiXeR, pleiotropy-informed locus discovery, colocalization, transcriptomic prioritization, single-cell projection, virtual knockout, and target annotation. Results Among 18 factor-disease comparisons, three survived FDR correction: an HDL-core axis positively correlated with AD (rg = 0.142, FDR = 0.002), a ketone-body axis inversely correlated with PD (rg = -0.106, FDR = 0.015), and a TG-rich/VLDL-remodeling axis inversely correlated with PD (rg = -0.072, FDR = 0.031). Component-level LDSC supported the biological traceability of these axes. Downstream analyses linked HDL-core/AD to perivascular support, ketone-body/PD to distributed neuronal-glial energy adaptation, and TG/VLDL-remodeling/PD to lysosomal and membrane-trafficking programs. Target annotation prioritized experimentally approachable genes including GRK4 , PRMT7 , and TMEM175 . Conclusions Structured metabolic genetic axes reveal selective and biologically distinct links between circulating metabolism and neurodegenerative disease, providing a framework for mechanism-focused follow-up beyond single-metabolite association.

items.title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
items.abstract_or_text: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.

items.title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.

items.title: Evidence-Grounded Large Language Model Reasoning for Patient Safety Using Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Development and Evaluation Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Large language models have shown substantial potential for supporting clinical reasoning, but their use in patient safety applications remains constrained by limited access to structured clinical knowledge, variable evidence grounding, and difficulty tracing generated reasoning to supporting sources. Knowledge graphs can provide structured representations of clinical and safety concepts, while retrieval-augmented generation can incorporate relevant biomedical evidence into model inputs. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated framework for evidence-grounded patient safety reasoning that combines a large language model, a patient-safety knowledge graph, and retrieval-augmented generation. The study examined how structured knowledge and evidence retrieval contribute to concept extraction and reasoning performance. Methods The framework was developed using adult intensive care data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III and MIMIC-IV. Patient safety concepts were normalized using established clinical terminology and patient safety classifications and represented within a structured knowledge graph. An LLaMA-based language model adapted using low-rank adaptation was used for concept extraction and reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation incorporated relevant biomedical literature, patient safety resources, clinical guidelines, and drug-related knowledge using biomedical sentence embeddings and a FAISS-based vector index. Retrieved evidence was ranked using cosine similarity and incorporated into the model context together with relevant graph information. Performance was evaluated using F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and area under the precision-recall curve. Component ablation analyses examined the effects of removing the knowledge graph, low-rank adaptation, and retrieval augmentation. Expert assessment also examined the relevance and usefulness of retrieved evidence and generated explanations. Results The full framework achieved an F1 score of 0.89 for concept extraction.
